content: Asthma is a chronic respiratory disease that affects over 300 million people globally, including both adults and children. It is characterized by symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. These symptoms are typically intermittent but can worsen rapidly, leading to an exacerbation. Asthma exacerbations can be severe, sometimes requiring hospitalization and, in rare cases, resulting in death. Treatment for exacerbations often involves increasing the patient’s usual medications and adding additional therapies, such as oral corticosteroids. Although antibiotics are occasionally used in these situations, bacterial infections are believed to account for only a small proportion of asthma exacerbations. Current clinical guidelines recommend reserving antibiotics for cases where there are clear signs, symptoms, or laboratory evidence of bacterial infection. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of antibiotics in treating asthma exacerbations. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Airways Trials Register, trial registries, and reference lists of primary studies, with the most recent search completed in October 2017. Studies were included if they compared antibiotic therapy to placebo or standard care without antibiotics in adults or children experiencing asthma exacerbations. The review included studies of any type, dose, or duration of antibiotics, provided the treatment was aimed at managing the exacerbation. Parallel studies of any duration and setting were included, while cross-over trials were excluded. Both published and unpublished data were considered. The review process involved at least two authors independently screening studies for eligibility, extracting data, and assessing the risk of bias. Discrepancies were resolved by consulting a third author. Data were analyzed using odds ratios (ORs), risk differences (RDs), and mean differences (MDs) with a fixed-effect model. Skewed data were described narratively. The quality of evidence was graded, and findings were summarized in tables. Primary outcomes included ICU or high-dependency unit (HDU) admission, duration of symptoms or exacerbations, and adverse events. Secondary outcomes included mortality, length of hospital stay, relapse rates, and peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR). Six studies met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 681 participants (adults and children) with asthma exacerbations. The mean age in the adult studies ranged from 36.2 to 41.2 years, while the pediatric studies included participants aged 1 to 18 years. Five studies explicitly excluded participants with clear signs of bacterial infection, aligning with current guidelines that recommend antibiotics only in such cases. Four studies investigated macrolide antibiotics, while two older studies (conducted over 35 years ago) examined penicillin-based antibiotics (amoxicillin and ampicillin). Five studies compared antibiotics to placebo, and one was an open-label trial. Follow-up periods ranged from one to twelve weeks. The methodological quality of the studies varied, and only limited meta-analysis was possible. None of the included studies reported ICU or HDU admissions. However, one child in the placebo group of a study involving children with status asthmaticus experienced respiratory arrest and required mechanical ventilation. Four studies reported asthma symptoms, but results could only be combined for two macrolide studies involving 416 participants. The mean difference in diary card symptom scores was -0.34 (95% CI -0.60 to -0.08), with lower scores indicating improved symptoms. Two macrolide studies reported on symptom-free days. In one study of 255 adults, the percentage of symptom-free days at 10 days was 16% in the antibiotic group compared to 8% in the placebo group. Another study of 40 children found significantly more symptom-free days in the antibiotic group compared to the usual care group. This same study also reported a shorter duration of the index exacerbation in the antibiotic group. One study involving penicillin antibiotics and 69 participants reported asthma symptoms at hospital discharge, but the between-group difference was not significant. Data on serious adverse events were combined from three studies involving 502 participants, but such events were rare, with only 10 reported (five in the antibiotic group and five in the placebo group). Data on all adverse events were also combined from three studies, but the effect estimate was imprecise (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.43). No deaths were reported in any of the included studies. Two studies investigating penicillins reported on hospital admission duration, but neither found a significant difference between groups. In one macrolide study involving 263 participants, two participants in each group experienced a relapse by the six-week follow-up. PEFR results at 10 days were combined for two macrolide studies, showing a mean difference favoring antibiotics over placebo (MD 23.42 L/min, 95% CI 5.23 to 41.60). One pediatric study reported the maximum peak flow during follow-up, favoring the clarithromycin group, but the confidence interval included no difference (MD 38.80, 95% CI -11.19 to 88.79). The quality of evidence ranged from moderate to very low, with downgrades due to concerns about publication bias, indirectness, imprecision, and poor methodological quality. The authors concluded that there is limited evidence suggesting antibiotics may improve symptoms and PEFR during follow-up compared to standard care or placebo. However, the findings were inconsistent across the six studies, two of which were conducted over 30 years ago. Most participants were recruited from emergency departments, limiting the generalizability of the results. There was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about several important outcomes, such as hospital admissions. While serious adverse events were rare, the review could not rule out differences between groups for all adverse events. Overall, the authors expressed limited confidence in the results.
